A shared ride around a disrupted commute

Portland commuters facing the southbound Interstate 5 closure through the Rose Quarter have another option for part of their journey: joining a group of cyclists headed toward downtown. The Portland Bureau of Transportation is offering Wednesday bike buses from North and Northeast Portland through October 14, according to reporting by OPB. These are scheduled group rides, with opportunities to join along the way, rather than a bus service carrying bicycles.

The closure provides the immediate reason for the extra rides, but the program also introduces people to commuting alongside other cyclists. Riders interviewed by OPB described several benefits: spending time with other people, feeling more comfortable on the road and avoiding the frustration of sitting in traffic. Those accounts reflect participants' experiences; the report does not establish how many car journeys the program has replaced.

How the routes work

The groups mainly follow neighborhood greenways and travel slowly. Riders can meet them at designated points along the route, and the groups arrive together at Salmon Street Springs downtown at 8:15 a.m. The special weekly schedule serves the north and northeast neighborhoods affected by the highway disruption. Six other routes in the wider bike bus program continue to operate monthly, so the Wednesday expansion should not be confused with a weekly schedule across the entire network.

PBOT has added live location tracking to the two special routes, allowing prospective participants to check the group's progress. There is also a small financial incentive for changing a commute: participants can receive five dollars in currency for use at the Shemanski Park Farmers Market. These additions accompany the temporary weekly rides; they do not establish that the city has permanently changed the program's schedule.

From a staff event to public participation

The program started inside city government in 2024. What was initially intended as a Bike Month event for employees proved popular enough to continue monthly through October of that year. It opened to the public in 2025. City workers and community volunteers have both helped lead rides during 2026. The response to the I-5 closure therefore builds on an existing program rather than introducing group commuting to Portland for the first time.

Room for different levels of experience

OPB spoke with Karin Wohlert, an established bicycle commuter who began joining the groups during the summer. She described appreciating both the social connection and the feeling of safety. The September 30 ride also included four-year-old Conor and his father, Aiden Forsi. Their school journey normally follows the same route, and they join when they encounter the bike bus. Forsi said other participants helped look out for Conor when they first rode with the group.

Volunteer leader Jack Gordon offered another perspective. Although he does not work downtown, he joined the September 30 northeast ride on a morning off because he enjoyed the company. He emphasized its relaxed character and slow pace. Together, these accounts show that participants have different reasons for joining: some are regular commuters, some are trying a group ride, and others value the social outing.

A connection within a longer journey

For some riders, the downtown meeting point is only one stage of a commute. Abby McFeeters-Krone leads a connecting group toward Nike's campus in Beaverton. She described using the city's existing program to help colleagues try riding to work in a supportive setting. Such journeys can combine cycling with MAX light rail. Her colleague Florin Veja usually cycles between Vancouver, Washington, and Beaverton, sometimes using MAX as well; September 30 was his first city bike bus outing.

What happens after the special rides

PBOT plans to assess the program when the season ends. Its review will consider routes, frequency, staffing and available resources before decisions are made for 2027. The current weekly service is therefore also a chance to learn about a more frequent schedule. OPB's report establishes the Wednesday rides through October 14, but it does not announce a permanent weekly expansion beyond that period.

Source: OPB. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked reporting.

Correction: An earlier version included unsupported statements about the closure's duration and ride leadership. Those statements have been removed, and the article has been revised for original wording.

A familiar Fresno name with a longer history

At First and Tulare streets, a bar and a nearby liquor store carry a name that prompted Fresnoland writer Vince Mancini to investigate: Uncle Tom's. His reporting traced the business to a candy shop established in 1921 and explored how it became a neighborhood gathering place. Behind the unusual name is a history involving the Licouris family, changes to the street and buildings, and customers who remained attached to the business after it moved.

The account combines Mancini's visits, interviews and historical newspaper material. It presents more than a story about a sign, but it also leaves some questions unresolved. In particular, the family explanation for the nickname does not establish everything the original owner might have understood or intended about its association with the title of Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel.

The shop that became a bar

The founder was Tom Licouris, originally from Licouria in Greece. His business began as Alta Vista Confectionary, selling candy and operating a soda fountain. His grandson, also named Tom Licouris, described the arrival of liquor after Prohibition ended in 1933 as the point when the family recognized that the operation had changed direction. The reporting connects the later bar and liquor store to that earlier confectionery rather than treating 1940 as the start of the business.

In 1940, the elder Licouris constructed a new building as First Street was widened. A contemporary advertisement described separate spaces for the bar and cafeteria and for retail sales, including alcohol, tobacco and sporting goods. The notice also said Licouris had already spent nineteen years in the local restaurant and liquor trade. Fresnoland uses those details to trace the establishment's roots back more than a century.

Changing buildings without losing every connection

The 1940 building was demolished in 1990. Fresnoland places the move into the newer shopping center behind it in 1991, when the family also sold the liquor store. The report includes memories of customers transferring their favorite stools to the replacement premises, a small detail that captures their attachment to the old location. Historical accounts of the move describe mixed feelings about losing the familiar building while hoping the replacement would work out.

The business passed through several generations. The founder died in 1954, and his son Peter continued the operation. The younger Tom later worked in the liquor store before moving into real estate. Peter died in 2004. These dates describe different parts of the family's involvement; they should not be combined into a single assumed date for the sale of both businesses.

The recollections behind the nickname

Tom Licouris the younger told Mancini that neighborhood residents called his grandfather Uncle Tom because of his friendly manner and the candy he gave children. That is the family's explanation for the personal nickname. It is less conclusive about the longer name, Uncle Tom's Cabin, which has also appeared in descriptions of the business. Licouris was very young when his grandfather died and could not fully resolve the reporter's questions about possible wordplay.

The grandson did acknowledge concern that people might interpret the name negatively. He recalled removing Cabin from the sign in 1990 and said the family had not received complaints about the name. Fresnoland notes that the longer version still appears in the website and map listing. The reporting therefore distinguishes the explanation offered by the family from questions that remain about the name's historical associations.

Customers, staff and the present-day business

Manager Tracy Valle described discovering the bar through family connections and later working there. She spoke about customers whose memories included accompanying a parent or grandparent to the area. Mancini's own visits found regulars with similar longstanding connections. These are individual accounts of the place's role in their lives, rather than evidence that everyone in the neighborhood shares the same view.

Valle identified the owners as Happy and Sonny. Her account and the younger Licouris's recollections use different relative descriptions of when the family stepped away, so they do not provide a sufficiently clear basis for assigning a precise ownership-change year here. The historical details are firmer: the confectionery roots in 1921, the new building in 1940, and the relocation around the demolition of the old premises.

Fresnoland's story shows how a question about a business name can uncover several layers of local history. Its interviews and newspaper research preserve memories of a gathering place while acknowledging that not every question about its past can be answered conclusively.

Source: Fresnoland. Prepared with AI assistance from the linked reporting.

Correction: An earlier version overstated what the family could establish about the name and the timing of ownership changes. This revision clarifies those uncertainties and replaces wording that was too close to the source.
